Circumlocution

/sur-kum-loh-KYOO-shun/ - the stress falls on KYOO · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Circumlocution means indirect and wordy language that avoids the point.

Ask Grandpa to borrow the truck and the circumlocution begins: twenty minutes on weather, tires, and responsibility, with never a yes or a no in it.

Worked Example

Dario called the warranty line with one question: covered, or not. Forty minutes later he had heard about policy tiers, seasonal claim volumes, and the company's founding promise of care — and still could not have said, under oath, whether the repair was covered. He hung up, dialed again, and asked for someone allowed to use short sentences.

Circumlocution is the exact word for what he sat through, because circumlocution means indirect and wordy language that avoids the point — the words circle the answer the way a moth circles a porch light, never landing. A digression wanders off the subject and comes back; circumlocution never leaves the subject and never arrives either.

How Circumlocution Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

wordiness

wordiness: too many words anywhere; circumlocution is wordiness with something to dodge

evasion

evasion: the dodge itself, by any means; circumlocution dodges with language

Antonyms

directness

directness: saying the thing straight

bluntness

bluntness: directness with the cushions removed

How Strong Is It? — hedging → circumlocution → stonewalling

hedging vs. circumlocution

hedging vs. circumlocution: Hedging pads the edges — a few maybes and mostlys around an answer that does, eventually, arrive.

stonewalling vs. circumlocution

stonewalling vs. circumlocution: Stonewalling goes further than circumlocution — circumlocution at least keeps talking around the point; stonewalling refuses to discuss it at all.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of circumlocution.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — circum-

Prefix — circum-: around

Root — locut

Root — locut: spoken (Latin loqui)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act of

Put it together

Put it together: Circum- (around) + locut- (spoken) + -ion (the act of) = the act of speaking around. Latin built the word exactly the way the habit works: the talk orbits the point without ever setting down on it.

Use the root in a new word: ventriloquist

Use the root in a new word: ventriloquist: A ventriloquist is literally a 'belly-speaker' — Latin venter (belly) + loqui (to speak) — throwing the voice so it seems to come from somewhere else.

Word Choice

formal / critical

Circumlocution judges: it says the speaker is dodging on purpose. Plain wordiness is only excess, and hedging is only caution. Keep it apart from this unit's digression — a digression leaves the subject and comes back; circumlocution never leaves the point, and never lands on it either.
